title: Uncorrelated perspectives
content:
After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing. The best books all emphasized the importance of owning a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated assets that rise and fall independently. If one crashes, the rest don’t.

Don’t put everything into stocks or real estate or commodities or any one market. Don’t put it all into America or Europe or Asia or any one place. Don’t over-invest in what’s popular or familiar. Invest equally into the entire world economy.

I apply this metaphor to worldviews.

You start with the perspective of your parents and culture. But you are over-invested in one or two worldviews. You have to deliberately diversify - to intentionally invest in other perspectives.

When your government or media says some country is the enemy, it’s a good sign that place has an uncorrelated perspective. The governments have conflicting interests, but the people there are not bad people. When another culture feels completely foreign, weird, and wrong, it means you are under-invested in that worldview.

Even in your own country, right versus left or whatever. When the “other side” seems crazy, you need to balance your portfolio. Invest some understanding until you hold some of those perspectives.

If people can predict your opinion on something, based on your opinion on something else, then your worldview is too correlated.

To be an independent thinker, own a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated perspectives.
author: Derek Sivers
